#### **A double blow**

Easter Monday, March 26, 1951

It must have been 10 o'clock in the morning when Dr Anne Casey, 36, started to worry. She had taken to the bed with pregnancy complications and little Laura was in with her now, bouncing on her big belly, and couldn't be stopped. Normally she'd go into her daddy in the other room, or be with her sister Jane, looking for the sweets he hid around the house. Anne hauled herself out of bed and waddled over to the mirror-image bedroom occupied by her husband, Dr Michael Augustine Casey, 52.

Austie Casey hadn't been in the best of health for some time and he'd already had two heart attacks. As soon as Anne opened the door, she let out a yelp, to the horror of the children and anyone else scattered around the house. There he was, dead to the world. He had slipped away in his sleep, painlessly she hoped.

The big house was curiously empty for a festive weekend. By now, Anne had taken to the other room because she was due to have the baby any day. We don't know what her physical difficulties were. Oedema, perhaps, or maybe toxemia. But things were definitely not looking good for the bambino. Laura Ann had been a miracle and was a ruddy two year old now, the first Rhesus baby in Ireland to survive. She got the all-important blood transfusion, a procedure that had only recently been developed in America. Austie Casey must have had to muscle his way through his medical contacts in Dublin as he managed to pull together a team who could save the baby. The chances of survival would be even lower for this bambino but there was still hope. Being so ill herself, and with her husband gone, Anne didn't have either the energy or the clout to pull together the right team for the coming birth. Alas, nine days later, the young widow would bear a still born baby, Joseph Patrick Casey, 0, and his little body would be buried beside his father in the loose soil of the family grave.

Jane was only four yet and remembers so much. How could you not? Richard was six and Michael, the eldest, was eight, his father's pride and joy. Now he would have to become the man of the house. Eventually, once the initial shock wore off and Anne came to she told Michael to run down and get the nanny. When no one came, Anne had to traipse down the stairs, her flock trailing behind her, to ask the maids where that aul wan was gone to. They said she was gone to Mass. The aul dragon! She's always gone to mass when she's wanted! Anne struggled back up the stairs and Michael went in with his mammy to see his father, and him there, gone.

#### **Enjoy it while you can**

(The next two paragraphs could be expanded into whole chapters, and may not be needed here yet).

The early years had been idyllic for the Casey family. The war was over, the world was opening back up, and the prosperous couple had begun to galavant. Austie Casey had, since his appointment in 1932, been the Medical Officer for the county town of Dungarvan. He was a dispensary doctor and Anne, who didn't have a post yet herself, helped make up the medicines, freeing Austie from that drudgery. It was time he did not waste. Incredibly, he was also the **managing director** of the town's two factories, both of which he had set up. In recent years, he found himself and his beautiful wife travelling all around America, buying machines and visiting family in Chicago and Los Angeles. Business was booming now and the men of Dungarvan had steady work, all year round, largely thanks to Austie Casey. The 1950s hadn't happened yet and the mood in Ireland was still hopeful. No sooner were the lovers back from The States and they went on a cruise to Portugal and Madeira. They had a nanny and three maids to help them raise the children, along with Granny May, Anne's mother.

After the tragedy, the four surviving children lived like stray cats, as Laura Ann remembers it, at least until the evening when they'd be home for their daily roast dinner. The older ones had more responsibility and had to face the horror head on. With no father, their mother would be flat out as a dispensary doctor, out in Gaeltacht area of Ring and Old Parish, working like a dog to keep the whole thing going. She only got a paltry stipend in accordance with Austie's second will, which had been changed after one of his heart attacks. **Soon enough, Austie Casey's siblings all began to drop, some of them afflicted by the same heart condition. In ten years' time, only one of the six was still alive. JOE?**

**Dungarvan Urban District Council**

Dungarvan is a small but rather self-sufficient town along the south coast of Ireland, thirty miles west of Waterford City and fifty miles east of Cork City. In the 1946 census, it had a population of 5,276 people, but a large hinterland and it was the seat of the Waterford county council, distinct then from the city council. Its geography looks remarkably similar to that of Dublin. It sits at the centre of a large, protected bay with a river splitting it into two unequal parts. To the north is the village and parish of Abbeyside while Dungarvan is to the south of the River Colligan, a fast-flowing river that rushes down from the mountains inland, also to one side, albeit to admittedly north. The farm land is very good in the hinterlands but there is no deepwater port so it never grew into a major trading post. Fishing has always been important in the area but even that began to dwindle in the early twentieth century. So in the 1930s, when Fianna Fail decided to dot factories all over the country, Dr Casey managed to convince them the Dungarvan was the perfect location for a tannery. With a river to provide clean water in, and the sea to wash away the noxious waste, its derelict quays were an ideal spot to locate the factory, despite the smell that would pervade the town for decades to come.

The following day, at noon, an emergency meeting was convened by the aforementioned council, known as the Dungarvan Urban District Council. Effusive tributes poured forth from several members present. While they recognised Dr Casey's considerate and painstaking work as a doctor in the town, they mostly saw him as their leading townsman and captain of local industry, the greatest industrialist Dungarvan has ever known. The man who was responsible for the town's industrial revival, with two flourishing factories. He gave employment, all the year round, to hundreds of men from the town and surrounding countryside, at the best of wages. Without Dr Casey, the town would not be as prosperous, as busy, or even as big as it is. He had been responsible for ending emigration from the town. By the time of the funeral, the following morning, Dr Casey had become perhaps the greatest industrialist in Munster, if not the country. Filling his shoes would be most difficult, if not impossible, although Austie's younger brother Percy, who did not attend the special meeting of the council that day, would soon try, before succumbing to heart failure six years later, also leaving behind a widow and some very young children.

It was noted that very few people realise the strenuous work that Austie had put into the starting of the two factories. This contemporary insight is crucial for our understanding of Austie Casey's role in establishing Dickens Leather factory back in 1935. Without it, one might argue that Austie Casey wasn't the greatest industrialist in even Dungarvan, as there were two bona fide leather men higher up the chain in that factory when it was established. The three of them demonstrate the three main groups who took part in Ireland's economic revolution in the 1930s. Austie Casey was one of the 'ruddy-faced gombeen men' of rural Ireland who oversaw the localization of industry around the country. There were the English capitalists looking to get into the newly protected Irish markets, and there were the Dublin-based professional class who liaised between the Brits and the provincial Irish.

Kennedy O'Brien, a Limerick man based in Dublin, would, over his lifetime, build a small empire across the South-East of Ireland, producing leathers and related products. He set up a hard leathers tannery in nearby Portlaw, making hard soles from cow hides, and Dungarvan was set up a year later as a complementary operation, tanning soft leathers from sheep hides for the softer, upper parts of the shoe. He was the managing director in Portlaw and the first Chairman in Dickens Leather.

Reginald Dickens, who gave his name to the Dungarvan tannery, hailed from Northampton, the heart of leather production in England and indeed the world. He was the managing director of the company. Dickens' father had set up a tannery around the turn of the century and it was taken over by the elder brothers. Reginald was a younger son who had to go and seek his fortune. When the newly formed Irish Free State began to place tariffs on imported goods, hoping to become a self-sufficient state, Reginald was among a band of opportunistic English industrialists who set up shop over here, in adherence with Fianna Fail's jealously regulated isolationist policies. Hoops had to be jumped through and loopholes had to be found, and no one was better at this than the lawyer, Arthur Cox, and the accountant Vincent Crowley, who was **Chairman** in Portlaw and on the first board of Dickens Leather.

The genius of Austie Casey was in getting a factory to Dungarvan at all. Once it was in the town he could muscle his way to the top and go on to set up a second, offshoot factory. While he couldn't bring the industry knowledge of a Dickens or an O'Brien, Austie Casey had the contacts in the Fianna Fail government of 1932 to convince them to give Dungarvan a factory. He knew Kennedy O'Brien through his Waterford circles, but he may well have known Lemass from his time in the IRA.

### **Mountain View House**

Mr and Mrs Michael Augustine Casey lived in a large Georgian house called Mountain View, on a two-acre plot just off O'Connell Street, as you head west out from the square, a few hundred metres. Despite being so close to the town centre, it feels like a country house, and, in its fine original state, it had space aplenty for a family doctor's duties by day and entertaining guests by night. However, it would certainly not have been equipped to deal with the sheer number of people who wanted to pay their respects to deceased before his removal on the Tuesday evening.

-   *The house has a quite formal entry hall, with a truly imposing entry port, a hefty ornate timber door in a wide, fan-lit surround with side glazing features also on the ornate side of the scale.*

-   To the right was a very long dining-room, twenty-six feet by fifteen, and it was separated by an arch from a drawing room with a huge fire place. I suspect that Austie's body would have been laid to rest

-   and there are seven bedrooms.

-   The finest two are at the front of the house, upstairs, with huge sash windows looking straight out at **Knockmealdown** mountain, to the admittedly north, making them slightly dreary, and lacking in restorative light energy. Outside, the house was covered all in ivy, head to toe, and around the beautiful non-original porch which has sadly been removed. The staff would have tended to the ample gardens which were walled off from the surroundings, leaving an idyllic space for Austie's young children to wander and play. They might enter in the back door

-   *Beyond, there’s an entry area with wood floor, and just beyond a stone floor section running the rest of the way through the rather deep property.*

-   The original residents, in 1815, were the Dower family, local scions of commerce and law. Eventually it would come to house the local Medical Officer and this is why it became the incongruously large home of a single man in his early thirties, Dr Michael Augustine Casey, at a time when young Anne Foley was in Ardmore, studying for the Leaving Certificate. The house came with the job, which was bad news for Anne, as Austie had never actually bought it. Instead, his money went into shares for the factory.

**Siblings**

Percy would have been the first to get to Mountain View. He was Austie's younger brother and had become is right hand man. He lived on the main street in Dungarvan and still oversaw the family business, a shop that had been owned by their father, Michael J., the much-loved champion of the town's poor, until his death in 1923, and later taken over by his equally-loved wife, Catherine, until her death in 1940. Both of them had huge funerals in the town. Together the Casey brothers set up the Glue and Gelatine factory during The War and, after Austie died, Percy would take on a lot of his responsibilities. He too would **become managing director** of Dickens Leather and would begin to build business connections abroad. Like their father, Percy would become a member of the county council before, like Austie, he would succumb to a heart attack in 1957, **aged just 50.**

The rest of them were as scattered as any large Irish family of the time. Cork, Dublin, England, America. May was married to a Dr Michael O'Shea, and they lived in his native Cork City. **Joe now lived in Los Angeles where he was a succesful accountant, and he would have jumped on the next available flight home. Joe, a highly successful accountant, had flown all the way from Los Angeles, where Austie and Anne had visited him on their tour of the States.** **Rennie, short for Lawrence, was a priest in Lancashire.** Rennie had come from Lancashire where he worked as part of a mission among the large Irish community, although he would retire with illness and see out his days in Mountain View, later that decade.

Dick was one of Austie's five surviving siblings. Joe and Fr Rennie were older while Percy and May were younger. **On this sad occasion,** Austie would be buried beside their little brother, John, who was only a few years younger than Austie but who had died aged 11, in 1917. **The first Michael died in infancy in 1892.**

The following evening, Austie Casey's body lay **IN STATE i**n Mountain View, a sizeable home **that had been housing doctors for decades**. (MORE) That evening, the coffin would be removed to St Mary's Parish Church, **half a mile away,** by a relay of workers from the Glue and Gelatine factory which had been set up during the war by Austie and his younger brother Pierce. The inputs to the glue factory were bi-products of the tanning done in the Dickens Leather factory since 1935, when Austie Casey, with his tireless organizational skills, managed to convince the powers that be in Dublin that the perfect place for a tannery would be Dungarvan. The factory was set up in the very heart of the town, where the river meets the sea.

## Funeral

Dungarvan shut down on the morning of the funeral and the place was so jammed that the car couldn't move through the crowd. Despite its size, the church couldn't accommodate all the mourners and hundreds had to stand in the precincts. Everyone could attend the burial immediately afterwards as the family plot was right by the entrance to the church. The people in attendance demonstrated the remarkably wide range of activities and contacts Austie had made in a life that paralleled perfectly the Irish nation in the first half of the twentieth century. A very large number in attendance would have been patients of Austie, for whom he had worked so painstakingly and conscientiously since his appointment as the local medical officer in **1932,** after a stint in nearby Cappoquin. There were the factory staff who had carried his body to the church the night before.

After that, the gathering was a diffuse, educated bunch, many of them leaders in the newly formed republic, hailing mostly from the East and South of the country. There were Austie's medical contacts, built up first in University College Dublin, where his studies overlapped with the Revolutionary Period of 1916-23, what he would have called The Troubles. His self-confessed involvement with the IRA in both Dublin and Waterford got him involved in politics and, in particular, Fianna Fail after their establishment and rise to power. It was through these contacts that, in 1935, he could organise the establishment of a large leather factory in Dungarvan, which Minister Sean Lemass would open. Several members attended from Dail Eireann and Seanad Eireann, along with officials from all public bodies in the country. Members of the Urban District Council attended as a single bloc, an agreement made at their emergency meeting on the Tuesday.

As a board member of two factories, Austie came into contact with many members of the legal and banking professions, and other managers and directors of various industrial concerns throughout the provinces of Munster and Leinster. It was through the work of such men that Ireland tried to fashion itself as a self-sufficient state, independent of Britain and scarcely connected by trade to Europe.

Austie's involvement in Gaelic games was honoured by the President of the GAA and very large attendance from the Gaels of Waterford, namely the people of the GAA community. **Austie played a huge role in local games.** This era was the high point of Waterford hurling and football. They won the All-Ireland hurling final in 1948 and 1949, with Dungarvan being the bulk suppliers, and the Waterfod Football team won...

In attendance also were also Garda and Army representatives in attendance; the latter may have gotten to know Austie through his eldest brother, Fr. Richard, who had been Head Chaplain in the army until 1948.

Dick would have surely driven down from Skerries where he had, by his energetic standards, retired into a posting as Parish Priest, a role he kept until his death in 1962. It is highly unlikely, given his profession, that he was at home for Easter when Austie died, although he certainly would continue to be a regular guest in Mountain View.

Astonishingly, Dick was the celebrant of the mass (a **Solemn Requiem and High mass**) and was joined by an enormous array of local priests, including those from parishes, to the east and north, of Kilgobnet, Abbeyside, Stradbally, Ballinameela, Kilrossanty, Touraneena, Fourmilewater, Rathgormac(k), Portlaw, and Carrick-on-Suir. From the west and south were priests from Ring and Old Parish, Ardmore, Clashmore, and Cappoquin. **Carriglea**? Other priets came from Kilkenny, England and Scotland.

The bulk of the mourners with Austie's patients and next most numerous were his employees.

## **Funeral**

Wednesday morning, 29 March, 1951

It's a **Wednesday** morning in late March and Dungarvan is dunta for the Doris Day. The busiest man in town has died and his funeral is today.

-   It's a curious irony that the now prosperous town has suspended business to celebrate the man who did more than anyone to bring work and wealth to the once-tough lives of people in a Free State town.

At his funeral today, it will be mentioned that Michael Augustine Casey, known as "Austie Casey", was "perhaps the greatest industrialist in Munster if not the country".
